slides.text: When radio contact with Ice Station Six ceased during the polar night, I was flown in by Coast Guard helicopter to investigate. The steel barracks were warm, stew was still simmering on the induction stove, and three parkas hung neatly by the airlock—meaning the three meteorologists had walked out onto the minus-fifty-degree ice pack in their shirtsleeves.

On the communications desk lay the station’s leather-bound hourly logbook. The final entry in Dr. Vane’s handwriting was dated November 14th—today—at 14:00 hours, ten minutes before our helicopter touched down: 'The knocking under the floorboards has stopped. Whatever came up through the ice core drill-shaft is wearing Miller’s face, and it hears the rotor blades.'

I felt the blood drain from my face and turned the page. There was one more entry, written in wet ink at 14:25 hours—fifteen minutes after I had entered the building alone while my pilot waited outside: 'The inspector is reading the logbook now. He hasn't noticed that the helicopter engines outside just shut off, or that there are four parkas hanging by the door.'
